analysis.one_liner: Partially extends ACA premium subsidies while cutting them, banning some covered care, and tightening hospital price transparency.
analysis.headline: The bill — which would extend enhanced ACA premium credits through 2031 while phasing them down 20% to 80%, add $10–$40 minimum monthly premiums, appropriate $15.5 billion for state reinsurance, and bar marketplace plans from covering gender-transition care — has sat in the Senate Finance Committee with zero cosponsors since its introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill bundles two very different things. It would extend the enhanced ACA premium tax credits that are otherwise set to expire, fund cost-sharing payments that lower out-of-pocket costs, pour billions into state reinsurance programs, and force hospitals, labs, and imaging providers to publish their real prices. But it would also cut the extended subsidies each year, make every subsidized enrollee pay at least $10–$40 a month, require photo ID to enroll, ban marketplace plans from covering gender-transition procedures, and restrict how federal subsidy dollars touch abortion coverage.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own insurance through the ACA marketplaces gain a multi-year extension of premium credits (eligibility temporarily stretched to households up to 700% of the poverty line), plus funded cost-sharing reductions that directly lower deductibles and copays for lower-income enrollees. States gain federal money for reinsurance that tends to hold down individual-market premiums. Patients paying cash gain published prices — including a discounted cash price providers must accept as payment in full — from hospitals, labs, imaging centers, and surgical centers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: ACA marketplace enrollees and cash-paying patients

how_it_helps.text: Extends the enhanced ACA premium tax credits through 2031 instead of letting them lapse, and for 2027–2031 opens eligibility to households with income up to 700% of the poverty line rather than 400% — though the extra help shrinks each year.
Appropriates 'such sums as may be necessary' to pay cost-sharing reductions for plan years beginning in 2026, which directly reduce deductibles and copays for lower-income marketplace enrollees.

Sends states $500 million for fiscal 2027 and $5 billion a year for 2028–2030 to set up reinsurance programs or 'invisible high-risk pools' that shift the cost of the sickest patients away from premiums, which tends to lower premiums for everyone else in the individual market.

Requires hospitals to publish monthly, in both plain-language and machine-readable formats, their gross charges, discounted cash prices, and payer-specific negotiated rates, with a senior-executive attestation and per-day civil penalties for noncompliance — including $500,000 to $10 million fines for repeat willful violators.

Extends the same price disclosure to clinical diagnostic labs, imaging providers, and ambulatory surgical centers beginning July 2027, and requires providers to accept the discounted cash price as payment in full from any cash-paying patient regardless of coverage.
Strengthens health-plan transparency duties: group health plan access to claims data, oversight of administrative service providers, plain-language explanations of benefits, and itemized bills.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the subsidy extension, the cost-sharing appropriations, and the $15.5 billion in reinsurance grants. Transgender patients lose marketplace coverage of gender-transition care, and the new subsidy accounts cannot pay for it or for abortion. People without government-issued photo ID face a new enrollment barrier. Every subsidized enrollee pays a new minimum premium of $10–$40 a month, and the enhanced subsidy itself is scheduled to shrink 20%, 40%, 60%, then 80% over the four years after 2027.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, plus patients losing covered services

drawbacks.text: The subsidy extension is designed to shrink: the enhanced amount is cut 20% in 2028, 40% in 2029, 60% in 2030, and 80% in 2031, and every subsidized enrollee must pay at least $10–$40 a month, so the bill restores only a declining fraction of the help that is expiring.

It bars all marketplace plans from covering gender-transition procedures and bars the new subsidy accounts from paying for them; the definitions sweep in vasectomy, hysterectomy, tubal ligation, mastectomy, and liposuction when done for gender transition, with exceptions only for intersex conditions, precocious puberty, male circumcision, and imminent physical danger.

It requires government-issued photo identification for every enrollee over 18 as a condition of enrollment verification — a documentation hurdle that tends to knock eligible people without ID out of coverage.

Starting in 2027, premium tax credits must be deposited into a new HSA-style 'Healthcare Affordability Account' that each enrollee must separately open and enroll in to receive their credit, adding a step in the enrollment process that risks people losing subsidies in the mechanics, and the account cannot be used for abortion or gender-transition care.

Plans covering abortion cannot count the abortion portion of the premium toward the tax credit and cannot receive any cost-sharing reduction payments, which would likely push abortion coverage out of the marketplace entirely.

The transparency penalties are modest relative to hospital finances — $300 per day for hospitals with 30 or fewer beds and $25–$35 per bed per day for the largest — though the bill does allow multi-million-dollar penalties for repeat knowing violations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The affordability pieces are real but smaller than the title suggests: the credit extension phases itself down to nearly nothing by 2031, adds minimum premiums, and is routed through a new account system that could trip people up. In exchange, the bill strips a specific category of care from all marketplace plans and adds ID verification barriers. The hospital and provider price-transparency title is the cleanest consumer win — real published prices, honored cash discounts, and escalating fines — though its fines are light for smaller facilities. As written, this is a partial, temporary subsidy extension traded for coverage restrictions on particular groups and a large new flow of federal money to insurers through reinsurance.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 9, 2025 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat without cosponsors, a hearing, or any vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Roger Marshall introduced the bill on December 9, 2025; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
No senator from either party has signed on as a cosponsor.
No further action of any kind appears in the record — no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost — the bill has not moved. If it stalls, the status quo wins: insurers and hospitals face no new transparency mandates, and marketplace enrollees are left waiting while the enhanced premium credits head toward expiration.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — nothing has moved

for.name: Sen. Roger Marshall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and is its only sponsor; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred; the bill's only support so far is its single Republican sponsor, with no cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill locks in private insurers as the permanent channel for subsidized coverage: extended premium credits and cost-sharing payments flow to them, and $15.5 billion in federal reinsurance grants would pay them for covering high-cost enrollees. In return, insurers take on new transparency and data-access duties, and consumers get lower premiums and out-of-pocket costs — but taxpayers foot the bill.

Hospitals must publish monthly, in consumer-friendly and machine-readable formats, their gross charges, discounted cash prices, and payer-specific negotiated rates — and must honor the cash price as payment in full. A senior executive must attest to accuracy, and fines run per day and reach $5–$10 million for repeat willful violations.

industries.industry: Clinical labs, imaging providers, and ambulatory surgical centers
industries.note: From July 2027 these providers must publish the same package of gross, cash, and negotiated prices, with per-day penalties for noncompliance. Their interest in keeping prices opaque runs directly against patients comparison-shopping for care.

Marketplace plans may not cover gender-transition procedures and the new subsidy accounts cannot pay for them, cutting these providers off from millions of insured patients and those patients from their care. Providers and patients lose together.

Federal subsidy dollars cannot be allocated to abortion coverage and plans covering abortion are cut off from cost-sharing reduction payments, likely ending abortion coverage in marketplace plans. Providers and the patients seeking this coverage lose together.

industries.industry: Health savings account custodians (banks and financial firms)
industries.note: Every subsidized marketplace enrollee would be required to open a Healthcare Affordability Account, a new mandated customer base for HSA custodians. The account adds an enrollment step for consumers and restricts what the money can buy.

analysis.trajectory: A one-sponsor bill with zero cosponsors and no committee action almost always dies in committee, and this one is likely to sit in the Senate Finance Committee. Its elements could resurface inside a larger health package if the scheduled expiration of enhanced premium credits forces a negotiation, but as introduced it has no evident path to a floor vote.
